headings.title: Introduction and Overview of the Ovarian Cycle
headings.content: The **ovarian cycle** is a series of monthly changes in the ovaries that prepare an egg for release and ready the body for a possible pregnancy. Lasting roughly twenty-eight days on average, this internal rhythm runs parallel to the uterine cycle, though the two are governed by entirely different sets of target tissues. The main job of the ovary is dual: to house and mature developing **follicles**, and to produce key sex hormones like **estrogen** and **progesterone**. Without this delicate interplay, normal reproductive health and fertility cannot be maintained.

headings.title: Follicular Phase: Development and Maturation
headings.content:
- **Primordial follicles**: Dormant structures present at birth, waiting for hormonal signals to start growing.
- **Primary and secondary stages**: The single layer of cells around the egg multiplies, forming fluid pockets and increasing in size.
- **Graafian follicle**: The mature, fluid-filled blister containing the fully developed oocyte right before it bursts open.

During this first half of the cycle, several follicles begin to wake up, but usually only one wins the race to become dominant. This chosen follicle nurses the egg and secretes rising tides of estrogen, which thickens the lining of the womb in preparation for potential implantation.

headings.title: Hormonal Control via the Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Ovarian Axis
headings.content: The brain and the ovaries talk to each other in a continuous feedback loop known as the **HPO axis**. The **hypothalamus** releases **gonadotropin-releasing hormone**, which tells the front part of the **pituitary gland** to secrete **follicle-stimulating hormone** and **luteinizing hormone**. These two pituitary hormones travel through the bloodstream to direct ovarian activity. In turn, the growing ovarian tissues pump estrogen and progesterone back to the brain to signal whether production should speed up or slow down.

headings.title: Ovulation: Mechanism and Physiological Triggers
headings.content: Ovulation is the dramatic climax of the follicular phase. As the dominant follicle secretes massive amounts of estrogen, it triggers a sudden, sharp spike in **luteinizing hormone** from the pituitary gland. This **LH surge** weakens the wall of the ovary, causing the mature follicle to rupture and eject the secondary oocyte into the pelvic cavity, where waiting fallopian tubes sweep it inside.

headings.title: Luteal Phase: Formation and Function of the Corpus Luteum
headings.content: Once the egg breaks free, the empty shell left behind inside the ovary transforms into a temporary yellow gland called the **corpus luteum**. Driven by continued luteinizing hormone stimulation, this structure becomes a hormone factory focused heavily on producing **progesterone** alongside smaller amounts of estrogen. Progesterone acts to secure and enrich the uterine lining, making it soft and nutrient-rich so a fertilized egg can safely implant.

headings.title: Fate of the Corpus Luteum: Menstruation versus Pregnancy
headings.content: The lifespan of the corpus luteum depends entirely on whether fertilization happens. If conception does not occur, the corpus luteum naturally withers away into a tiny white scar called the **corpus albicans**, causing progesterone levels to crash and triggering **menstruation**. If a fertilized embryo implants, it releases **human chorionic gonadotropin**, a chemical messenger that tricks the corpus luteum into staying alive and continuing to pump out progesterone to support the early pregnancy.

headings.title: Clinical Implications and Common Cycle Disorders
headings.content: Disruptions in the ovarian cycle can lead to significant health and fertility challenges. Conditions like **polycystic ovary syndrome** feature hormonal imbalances that prevent normal ovulation, leading to irregular periods and elevated male hormone levels. Stress, extreme weight loss, and thyroid problems can also shut down the hypothalamus, stopping the cycle altogether. Nurses must understand these patterns to help patients navigate fertility assessments and hormonal treatments.
